summary:
Ladakh stands under India's national framework as rewritten by the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, which India's Parliament passed in March 2026. The amendment removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court of India's 2014 judgment, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals, and mandates medical certification for identity recognition. Human Rights Watch called the bill a major setback that strips thousands of their rights and increases their risk. Self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people fall outside the recognition scheme, so a trans visitor's identity-document practice in Ladakh rests on medical certification rather than on self-declaration.

BBC News reported that both houses of Parliament approved the amendment to the 2019 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act and that it awaited presidential assent. Opposition parties and the LGBTQ community protested the change. The government states that the amendment widens access to welfare benefits; critics answer that it excludes transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people. Recognition remains uneven, and the discrimination it produces is reported in education, healthcare and formal employment.

Ladakh is a union territory without its own legislature, reconstituted in 2019 from the former state of Jammu and Kashmir, so trans-related policy and recognition rules here are set by the central government in New Delhi. There is no sub-national route in Ladakh to soften or extend the national recognition scheme.

The entry and stay baseline is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity; the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. No same-sex marriage or civil partnership exists, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities.

Access to transition-related care is governed nationally: the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. Bans on conversion therapy from the Madras High Court judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.
tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 amendment was contested before and after passage. Opposition parties and LGBTQ community members protested; rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Human Rights Watch's assessment that the bill is a major setback places India's recognition regime in worse standing than the self-identification route the 2014 Supreme Court judgment established.

India has an estimated two million transgender people, which sets the scale of the population affected by the recognition limits, and discrimination in education, healthcare and formal employment is reported as continuing alongside them. The pattern of checkpoint and custody friction described in the sources runs through several states rather than one: airport interception in Chennai, a station allegation in Kolkata, custody treatment in Assam, and passport-authority demands for a medical examination litigated in Allahabad in February 2026. None of these incidents is recorded in Ladakh itself.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ladakh are covered by welfare and healthcare provisions set outside the union territory. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras; these boards are structures of other states, not of Ladakh.

The Ayushman Bharat scheme expansion of April 2024 makes transition-related healthcare available to all members of the transgender community under the national health insurance scheme. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

The Madras High Court's 7 June 2021 judgment in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police binds police conduct through its guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons and sensitisation, and directs the National Medical Commission and education authorities; its conversion-therapy ban and the National Medical Commission's 2022 ban operate alongside clandestine networks that continue to function.

Constitutional protection for residents rests on the Supreme Court of India's reading of Article 15 as prohibiting discrimination by sex, extended by the Allahabad High Court in 2021 to employment. Intersex infants remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: BBC News reported on 26 March 2026 that the amendment awaited presidential assent. Whether it has since received assent, and so whether it is in force in Ladakh today, is not established by the sources held here.

Not sourced: whether Ladakh operates its own transgender welfare board, designated shelter, or gender-affordant healthcare facility. The welfare-board structures described in the inventory belong to Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha, and the sources do not state what provision, if any, the union territory administration makes.

Unresolved: whether the divergence in police-conduct assessments applies to Ladakh. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note and the June 2024 victim interviews do not identify Ladakh, and no source held here reports police treatment of trans people in the union territory.

Not sourced: any trans-specific incident, arrest, medical screening demand or documentation refusal occurring in Ladakh, and any intersex surgery practice there. The incidents cited in the sources took place in Chennai, Kolkata, Assam and, in litigation, before the Allahabad High Court.
